about: Candidate kinds for each OpenAntiquity feature class, drawn from the FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types.

fields.term, id, uri, scope_note, thesaurus_cla: as the version 29 tables give them
fields.narrower_of_class_term: true when the thesaurus files the term directly beneath the class's own term
fields.lidar: our judgement, not the thesaurus's: S, its form could be told from its siblings in one-metre LIDAR; P, sometimes; N, not without excavation, standing fabric, finds or documents. Untested against data
fields.proposed_kinds: the kinds proposed to the owner on 2026-11-14 in docs/plans/kinds-of-feature.md; a proposal, not a decision

term.scope_note: An area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or other similar barrier. Use specific type where known.

candidates.scope_note: A monument consisting of a small (generally less than 100m diameter) subcircular enclosure with a narrow approach way consisting of parallel ditches (thus banjo shaped). Believed to be associated with stock management in the Later Prehistoric period.
candidates.lidar_reason: small sub-circular enclosure with a parallel-ditched approach is a distinct plan

candidates.scope_note: A Neolithic monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by frequent causeways, and often accompanied by an internal bank, also causewayed.
candidates.lidar_reason: interrupted circuits show where they survive as earthworks; most are ploughed flat

candidates.scope_note: A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the boundary follows an irregular curving course.
An enclosed area of land of varying size and shape which shows traces of defence.
candidates.lidar_reason: substantial banks suggest defence; 'defence' is an interpretation

candidates.scope_note: An area of land enclosed by one or several boundary ditches. Double index with a term to indicate the shape of the enclosure where known.
candidates.lidar_reason: ditch without bank can show as a hollow; often cropmark only

candidates.scope_note: An enclosure where the boundary consists of a line of discrete pits, as opposed to a continuous ditch. Use with a term that describes the shape of the monument.
candidates.lidar_reason: discrete pits rarely survive as visible hollows

candidates.scope_note: A rectangular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier consists of several straight or near straight sections.
A small circular enclosure defined by a turf or earthern bank.
An enclosure surrounded by a wooden stockade. A rare site type of Neolithic date.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows an almost rectangular course.

A large hilltop or hillslope enclosure in South West England, located close to rock outcrops, and surrounded by one or more circuits of stone built walls. All are prehistoric; some are definitely Neolithic.
candidates.lidar_reason: stone circuits by tors can show; date and type need fieldwork

term.scope_note: A hilltop enclosure bounded by one or more substantial banks, ramparts and ditches. Use more specific type where known.

candidates.scope_note: A hilltop enclosure bounded by a double line of ramparts.
Hillslope forts with wide spaced ramparts.
candidates.lidar_reason: widely spaced ramparts on a slope

candidates.scope_note: A hillfort enclosure with defences composed of more than one bank and ditch.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a single rampart, usually accompanied by a ditch.
A defensive enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a neck of land, in order to defend, or restrict access to, a spur or promontory, either inland or on the coast.

An enclosure defined by a single bank and entrance. They occur on every type of ground, although they favour sheltered, valley side locations. Smaller and usually less well defended than hillforts they are thought to be settlements of Iron Age date.
candidates.lidar_reason: single bank on a slope; date is inferred

candidates.scope_note: A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.
candidates.lidar_reason: slight univallate circuit; told from a hillfort by scale

candidates.scope_note: A small, Iron Age/Romano-British enclosed settlement found in South West England.
candidates.lidar_reason: small enclosure in the South West; type is regional and dated

candidates.scope_note: An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
candidates.lidar_reason: an interpretation of status and date

term.scope_note: Hemispherical mound surrounded by a ditch (or occasionally two or more concentric ditches), often accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank. Mound and ditch may sometimes be separated by a berm. Use specific type where known.

candidates.scope_note: A round barrow in which the mound and ditch are separated from each other by a berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
A form of round barrow intermediate between the Bell Barrow and the Disc Barrow. Only use where it is not possible to determine specific type.
A round barrow featuring a mound surrounded by a ditch, with no intervening berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external bank.
candidates.lidar_reason: mound and ditch with no berm

candidates.scope_note: A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
A round barrow featuring a small mound separated from a ditch of much greater diameter by a wide berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
candidates.lidar_reason: small mound, wide berm, large ditch

candidates.scope_note: The rarest of the recognized types of round barrow, consisting of a flat, wide circular mound, which may be surrounded by a ditch. They occur widely across southern England with a marked concentration in East and West Sussex.
candidates.lidar_reason: flat wide mound; can be confused with other platforms

candidates.scope_note: A round barrow featuring a low, wide mound surrounded by a ditch which may be accompanied by an external bank.
A monument featuring an artificial circular shallow depression surrounded by a bank which runs around the rim of the depression.
candidates.lidar_reason: a hollow with a rim bank

candidates.scope_note: A circular bank surrounding an area where burials were placed.
candidates.lidar_reason: circular bank around a flat interior

candidates.scope_note: A burial monument, usually of Iron age date, comprising a small square ditched enclosure surrounding a central interment, which may also have been covered by a mound.
candidates.lidar_reason: small square ditch; usually ploughed out

candidates.scope_note: Circular or near circular ditches, usually seen as cropmarks. Use the term where the function is unknown. Ring ditches may be the remains of ploughed out round barrows, round houses, or of modern features such as searchlight emplacements.
candidates.lidar_reason: circular ditch, usually a cropmark; LIDAR shows it only as a slight hollow

candidates.scope_note: A roughly hemispherical mound constructed primarily of stones, normally containing or covering one or more human burials. The mound may be surrounded and partly retained by a low stone kerb.
candidates.lidar_reason: stony mound; material needs ground check or imagery

candidates.scope_note: A low, wide, circular ring or bank of stones surrounding an open, roughly circular area which is (or was initially) free of cairn material. The inner and outer faces of the bank may be kerbed.
candidates.lidar_reason: ring of stones round an open centre; material needs ground check

candidates.scope_note: A cluster of closely spaced barrows and related monuments (eg. ring ditches). Use with specific barrow-types where known.
A natural or artificial elevation of earth or stones, such as the earth heaped upon a grave. Use more specific type where known.

term.scope_note: A rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound of Neolithic date, usually accompanied by flanking or encircling ditches, and normally associated with human remains. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.

candidates.scope_note: A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.
candidates.lidar_reason: chamber is internal, though stones may show at one end

candidates.scope_note: A form of Neolithic long barrow comprising an oval, rather than rectangular or trapezoidal mound.

A poorly understood Neolithic monument comprising a very long, narrow earthen mound. They may be of single-phase construction, or represent the addition of a linear extension to the bank of an existing Long Barrow.
A long, narrow mound of earth or stone and of uncertain date and function. Use more appropriate term where possible.

A rectangular or trapezoidal non-megalithic stony mound of Neolithic date, with human remains in cists rather than a large chamber. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.
candidates.lidar_reason: stony mound; material needs ground check

candidates.scope_note: A subrectangular earthen enclosure defined by a ditch, usually with an internal bank, assumed to have been used for the primary exposure or burial of human remains in the Neolithic period prior to secondary burial elsewhere.
candidates.lidar_reason: function is an interpretation; form is a small subrectangular enclosure

term.scope_note: A round house indicated by the presence of a low, roughly circular bank of turf, earth or stone, which formed the base of the walls. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Where several occur together use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT.

candidates.scope_note: A settlement consisting of several hut circles, either grouped together or dispersed. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Use specific forms where supported by the available evidence. For isolated hut circles use HUT CIRCLE.
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.

A settlement with evidence for several hut circles but clearly lacking an obvious boundary. Where it is not certain whether a boundary existed or not, use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
Circular structure, normally indicated by one or more rings of post holes and/or a circular gulley, and usually interpreted as being of domestic function.
candidates.lidar_reason: post-hole rings and gullies are below ground

candidates.scope_note: Levelled or terraced area of ground presumed to have been the site of a house or hut.

Circular or near circular ditches, usually seen as cropmarks. Use the term where the function is unknown. Ring ditches may be the remains of ploughed out round barrows, round houses, or of modern features such as searchlight emplacements.
candidates.lidar_reason: circular ditch, usually a cropmark; LIDAR shows it only as a slight hollow

candidates.scope_note: Circular enclosure featuring an enclosing bank with no accompanying ditch. Use specific type where known.
A low, wide, circular ring or bank of stones surrounding an open, roughly circular area which is (or was initially) free of cairn material. The inner and outer faces of the bank may be kerbed.
candidates.lidar_reason: ring of stones round an open centre; material needs ground check

term.scope_note: A small concentration of dwellings.

candidates.scope_note: A civil and administrative area incorporating a town of medieval origin.
Temporary settlement relating to the construction of railways, viaducts, dams, etc.
An island, partly or wholly artificial, built up by dumping timber, earth and stones onto a lake or river bed. Often revetted with timber piles or palisade.
candidates.lidar_reason: island in a lake or former lake

candidates.scope_note: An abandoned settlement, usually of the Medieval period, often visible only as earthworks or on aerial photographs.
candidates.lidar_reason: earthworks of tofts, crofts and hollow ways

candidates.scope_note: A camp where people who fled from danger or problem whithin their country or across international borders and who are in need of international protection are temporarily placed.

A site used primarily for domestic purposes on at least a semi-permanent or seasonal basis, and which has been surrounded by a bank and ditch, palisade, or some other form of enclosure. Use more specific type(s) where appropriate.
A suburb of a town, especially Roman or Medieval, situtated or extending beyond its formal limits, usually demarked by defences.
candidates.lidar_reason: relation to a town's defences and documents

candidates.scope_note: Small settlement with no ecclesiastical or lay administrative function.
candidates.lidar_reason: a matter of size and administration

candidates.scope_note: A small settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling with ancillary buildings.
A residential district planned as a unit.

A settlement consisting of several hut circles, either grouped together or dispersed. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Use specific forms where supported by the available evidence. For isolated hut circles use HUT CIRCLE.
A settlement located on or near to the shores of a lake. Buildings associated with lake villages are usually raised on piles to prevent them from being flooded.
A group of related buildings, primarily with a domestic function, which is arranged along a principle axis such as a main road or routeway.
candidates.lidar_reason: house sites strung along a road

candidates.scope_note: A planned village or settlement, usually developed by a philanthropic industrialist , to house workers. Most include facilities for the education and betterment of the workers and their families.
Residential area built to house athletes and their coaches at the Olympic Games. The buildings are generally reused as public housing after the contest.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic occupation site, excluding occupations of caves and rock shelters. Evidence for occupation may include traces of hearths and other structures.
A settlement located on or near a river or within marshy landscapes. This type of settlement are raised on piles to prevent flooding.
A settlement built to a pre-determined plan, including housing, infrastructure and associated amenities.
candidates.lidar_reason: regular plots can show; intent needs documents

candidates.scope_note: A temporary settlement established as a public protest against an aspect of government policy or more specifically the development of a site.
A temporary settlement or shanty-town erected by railway construction workers or navvys.""
A camp for the temporary accommodation of uprooted civilians or foreign ex-service personnel, who had fought for the British forces during WWII (e.g.Polish).
A settlement, usually enclosed, on a sloping hillside containing a number of oval or circular scopped house floors separated by walls or unexcavated ridges.
candidates.lidar_reason: house scoops cut into a slope

candidates.scope_note: A site occupied by people who have no legal right to the land or buildings on it.
A largely residential area on the outskirts of a town or city.
A parcel of land.
An assemblage of public and private buildings, larger than a village and having more complete and independent local government.
Cluster of dwellings of medieval or later date (Scots)
A settlement used for trading.
A settlement without any obvious evidence for a boundary. Use specific type where known.
A district, suburb or quarter of a town or village adjacent to a fort, with the lowest legal status accorded to a built up area.
candidates.lidar_reason: legal status and relation to a fort

candidates.scope_note: Small discreet rural settlements which do not provide the commercial, legal or ecclesiastical services typically found within medieval urban areas.
A collection of dwelling-houses and other buildings, usually larger than a hamlet but smaller than a town with a simpler organisation and administration than the latter.
candidates.lidar_reason: a matter of size and administration

candidates.scope_note: A temporary settlement or encampment erected by construction workers (eg for reservoir construction).
A settlement where previous house sites are now unoccupied, but often visible as earthworks, crop or soil marks.
The place where a house stood or had once stood, often adjoining a garth or croft.
candidates.lidar_reason: house site, often a platform in a plot

candidates.scope_note: An enclosed piece of land adjoining a house.
An area of ground on which a house is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a house.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
candidates.lidar_reason: long building footing on a slope; byre end needs fieldwork

term.scope_note: A structure with a roof to provide shelter from the weather for occupants or contents. Use specific type where known.

candidates.scope_note: A structure which can be an area within a building, a separate building within a complex or a detached architectural component of a building
A gateway with one or more chambers over the entrance arch; the flanking towers housing stairs and additional rooms. Use with wider site type where known.
A small building used by a gatekeeper.
Building or buildings housing equipment for generating heat for a building complex.
A building or room where business, administrative or professional activities are conducted. Use specific type where known.
A detached subordinate building. Use specific type where known, eg. DAIRY.
candidates.lidar_reason: a small footing near a larger one

candidates.scope_note: Prefabricated small building that is designed and built to be movable rather than permanently located.
A small building used by the keeper of a castle, park, etc.
A slight structure built for shelter or storage, or for use as a workshop, either attached as a lean-to to a permanent building or separate. Use more specific type where known.
A building in which goods or items are stored. Use more specific type where known.

A tall building, either round, square or polygonal in plan, used for a variety of purposes, including defence, as a landmark, for the hanging of bells, industrial functions, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A tall, multi storeyed building either used as business premises or, more usually, as residential accomodation.
A free-standing building or a room used as a storage place for valuable objects.
A building for human habitation, especially a dwelling place. Use more specific type where known.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
candidates.lidar_reason: long building footing on a slope; byre end needs fieldwork

candidates.scope_note: The place where a house stood or had once stood, often adjoining a garth or croft.
candidates.lidar_reason: house site, often a platform in a plot

candidates.scope_note: The homestead of a farm consisting of a farmhouse and working farm buildings, with yards, other working areas and usually a garden to the house.
candidates.lidar_reason: a cluster of footings and yards

candidates.scope_note: A building for the storage and processing of grain crops and for housing straw, farm equipment and occasionally livestock and their fodder. Use more specific type where known.
A freestanding building, or a room or recess serving as a place of Christian worship in a church or other building. Use more specific type where known.
A building used for public Christian worship. Use more specific type where known.
The principal house of a manor or village.
A building with an aisle along one or both sides. Usually a row of posts separates the main space from the aisle.

term.scope_note: A group or complex of fields which appear to form a coherent whole. Use more specific type where known.

candidates.scope_note: A field system which appears to have developed in an organic, or piecemeal, fashion over time.

A fairly regular system of small rectangular fields. Examples may date from the middle Bronze Age to the Roman period. The word 'Celtic' carries no chronological or cultural connotations in this context.
candidates.lidar_reason: small regular rectangular fields with lynchets

candidates.scope_note: An area of land which retains distinctive large-scale rectilinear land divisions characteristic of Roman agriculture. Generally aligned with the course of a Roman road.
candidates.lidar_reason: large-scale grid aligned on a Roman road; hard to prove

candidates.scope_note: A field system with one prevailing axis of orientation, in which most field boundaries are either aligned with this axis or run at right angles to it.

Medieval Fenland ditched field system where the land is divided into strips for agricultural production. The strips are separated by hand-dug wide shallow drainage ditches with the spoil thrown up to create a dryer ridge.
A system of individually enclosed fields.
An area of arable land with common rights after harvest or while fallow. Usually without internal divisions (hedges, walls or fences).
candidates.lidar_reason: shown by ridge and furrow in furlongs; rights need documents

candidates.scope_note: Grassland fertilized by allowing floodwater to cover it in winter.
A bank formed at the end of a field by soil which, loosened by the plough, gradually moves down slope through a combination of gravity and erosion.
candidates.lidar_reason: scarp at a field edge on a slope

candidates.scope_note: A terraced field usually found on hillsides. Comprising a flat strip of land, called the tread, and a steep, scarped lynchet or edge, called the riser.
An area of land, usually on a slope, which has been built up to provide a flat surface for the cultivation of crops.
Areas used for potato-growing.
Narrow ridges representing the surviving surface traces of later prehistoric cultivation.
The limit line of a field.
An area of agriculturally used land, which is divided into small, elongated, rectangular fields running parallel to each other.
A group of cairns occurring within close proximity to each other. Use for instances where the majority are clearance cairns. Also index specific types where known.
An irregularly constructed, generally unstructured, mound of stones. Often, but not necessarily, circular. Normally a by product of field clearance for agricultural purposes.
candidates.lidar_reason: small stony mound; told from a burial cairn by fieldwork

term.scope_note: A series of long, raised ridges separated by ditches used to prepare the ground for arable cultivation. This was a technique, characteristic of the medieval period.

candidates.scope_note: Long parallel soil ridges in excess of 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
Long parallel soil ridges less than 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
A ridge and furrow produced by a plough drawn between two steam engined vehicles, or a steam engined vehicle and a moveable windlass, standing on opposite headlands.
candidates.lidar_reason: straight, very regular narrow rig; told from narrow ridge and furrow mainly by straightness and setting

candidates.scope_note: Narrow ridges representing the surviving surface traces of later prehistoric cultivation.
A narrow strip of land where a plough and team could turn. This usually remains higher than the ploughed land.
candidates.lidar_reason: raised strip at the end of ridges

candidates.scope_note: Areas used for potato-growing.

term.scope_note: A substantial bank and ditch forming a major boundary between two adjacent landholdings. Most date from the late Bronze Age and Iron Age.

candidates.scope_note: A multiple, parallel arrangement of linear earthwork ditches, usually accompanied by banks, and often of considerable territorial extent. Usually of later prehistoric or Roman date.
A linear earthwork, usually a bank accompanied by a ditch, which runs across rather than along an area or ridge of higher ground.
candidates.lidar_reason: bank and ditch across a ridge

candidates.scope_note: A defensive or boundary earthwork.
candidates.lidar_reason: large bank and ditch; defence is an interpretation

candidates.scope_note: An earthen bank that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A ditch that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A system of long, continuous banks and/or ditches dividing land into well defined areas. Possibly used for controlling livestock
candidates.lidar_reason: long banks and ditches dividing land; date needed

candidates.scope_note: A stone wall, often of considerable length, built to divide an area of land. Most occur as part of extensive walled field systems. This is a regional term specific to Dartmoor and should not be used in other parts of the country.
candidates.lidar_reason: stone wall; regional to Dartmoor by the scope note

candidates.scope_note: A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.
candidates.lidar_reason: the fence is gone; the bank and internal ditch can show

candidates.scope_note: An earthen bank indicating the limit of a wood or coppice
candidates.lidar_reason: bank round a wood; context tells it apart

candidates.scope_note: Linear or curvilinear construction of earth, turf and stone, often, but not always accompanied by a ditch. Use specific type where known.
A long and narrow hollow or trench dug in the ground, often used to carry water though it may be dry for much of the year.
A length of straight, curved or angled earthwork or cropmark of uncertain date or function.
A single line, or pair of roughly parallel lines, of pits set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes. The pits are not thought to have held posts.

Ditches interrupted by wide, regular causeways. Each section of ditch is about 30-40m long, and each causeway is 10-15m wide. In some cases, a network of fields has been created. Found mainly in the South East of England.

term.scope_note: A pathway, not necessarily designed as such, beaten down by the feet of travellers.

candidates.scope_note: A path, barred to vehicles, reserved for riding horses.
A trackway through blanket bog constructed to create a dry route. Formed by removing peat to link areas already eroded to the granite bedrock.
A track of two parallel ruts deliberately cut in the ground or living rock for the guidance of two-wheeled carts when the way was obscured by darkness or water.
candidates.lidar_reason: paired ruts can show where cut in rock

candidates.scope_note: A way, path or road through a cutting.
A road or track specifically used by drovers or herders to drive their animals to market.
candidates.lidar_reason: wide verges and banks; use needs documents

candidates.scope_note: Narrow, rough tracks often over upland routes used by packhorse trains to carry goods.
candidates.lidar_reason: narrow upland route; use needs documents

candidates.scope_note: A road or pathway raised above surrounding low, wet or uneven ground.
A road, used traditionally for the transportation of a corpse to a place of burial.

term.scope_note: A way between different places, used by horses, travellers on foot and vehicles.

candidates.scope_note: A passageway or lane between buildings.
A road, sometimes raised as a causeway, which serves as an approach road to a building or bridge.
candidates.lidar_reason: a raised route to a building or bridge

candidates.scope_note: A wide street, traditionally lined with trees.
A road or street covered with small, rounded cobble stones.
A road or track specifically used by drovers or herders to drive their animals to market.
candidates.lidar_reason: wide verges and banks; use needs documents

candidates.scope_note: A way, path or road through a cutting.
A road used primarily, but not exclusively, for the rapid transport of military vehicles, equipment and personnel.
Fast arterial road with separate carriageways limited to motor vehicles
Narrow, rough tracks often over upland routes used by packhorse trains to carry goods.
candidates.lidar_reason: narrow upland route; use needs documents

candidates.scope_note: The central part of a road between the pavements or the verges.
A road whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
A pathway, not necessarily designed as such, beaten down by the feet of travellers.
candidates.lidar_reason: worn route, often a hollow way

candidates.scope_note: A road surface made out of wooden blocks or planks. It was much used in English cities before 1940, but the cost of wooden blocks eventually made it uneconomical.
A long ridge of earth, rocks or gravel primarily constructed to carry a roadway.
A road or pathway raised above surrounding low, wet or uneven ground.

term.scope_note: A wide ditch surrounding a building, usually filled with water. Use for moated sites, not defensive moats. Use with relevant site type where known, eg. MANOR HOUSE, GARDEN, etc.

candidates.scope_note: A pond used for the rearing, breeding, sorting and storing of fish.
candidates.lidar_reason: rectangular ponds, often in sets with dams

candidates.scope_note: A dry ditch or sunken fence which divided the formal garden from the landscaped park without interrupting the view.
candidates.lidar_reason: sunk ditch with one vertical side between garden and park

candidates.scope_note: The principal house of a manor or village.

term.scope_note: An artificial steep-sided earthen mound on, or in, which is set the principal tower of a castle.

candidates.scope_note: An early form of castle consisting of a flat-top steep-sided earthen mound, supporting a wooden tower, and a bailey.
A defensive bank and ditch, circular or oval in plan, surrounding one or more buildings.
candidates.lidar_reason: circular bank and ditch round a space

candidates.scope_note: An enclosure within a bailey which contained a keep and sometimes took the place of a motte.
The courtyard of a castle, ie. the area enclosed by the rampart or curtain. Use with wider site type where known.
An artificial mound of earth indicating either the former site of a windmill or built as the base of a post windmill.
candidates.lidar_reason: small mound, often with cross-trench scars

candidates.scope_note: An artificial mound, generally conical, placed within a garden or park to provide a viewing point to overlook the garden or park. It may also serve as a visual focus in the garden or park layout.
candidates.lidar_reason: conical garden mound; context tells it apart

term.scope_note: A site where a building once stood as identified by a level area of ground, often compacted or made from man-made materials. Use only where specific function is unknown, otherwise use more specific term.

candidates.scope_note: A levelled area of ground on which a barn is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a barn.
candidates.lidar_reason: a barn needs fabric or documents

candidates.scope_note: An area of ground on which a house is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a house.
Levelled or terraced area of ground presumed to have been the site of a house or hut.
Unspecified. Use specific type where known.
A levelled area of ground, circular in shape, used as the base on which a monument was built.Sometimes raised, a platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a monument.
An area of flattened or compacted ground used for charcoal burning.
candidates.lidar_reason: small circular level stance in woodland on a slope

term.scope_note: A body of still water often artificially formed for a specific purpose. Use specifc type where known.

candidates.scope_note: A pond used for dissipating heat by evaporation from steam engine condensate. Mid 19th century to mid 20th century.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
A shallow pond, often artificial, fed by the condensation of water from the air, occuring on high land which has no other adequate water supply.
candidates.lidar_reason: small round embanked pond on high ground

candidates.scope_note: A small pond, usually circular and serving as a feature at the centre of a walled garden, used for the purpose of filling watering cans.
A pond with protection for nesting ducks and other wild fowl
A pond used for the punishment, by ducking in water, of offenders.
A pond used for the rearing, breeding, sorting and storing of fish.
candidates.lidar_reason: rectangular ponds, often in sets with dams

candidates.scope_note: A pond used as a water supply for the operation of a furnace or blast furnace.
Pond, created specifically for providing power to water-powered forges, blast furnaces, helve or other hammers.
candidates.lidar_reason: pond held by a large dam in a valley; use needs documents

candidates.scope_note: A shallow pond, often located near an ICEHOUSE, built to provide ice during the winter.
A water pond in which lilies are grown.
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
The area of water retained above a mill dam for driving a mill.
candidates.lidar_reason: pond behind a dam near a mill

candidates.scope_note: An ornamental garden feature, sometimes with an associated bath house.
A small artificial pond of water often found in parks and gardens, for decorative purposes.
A pond storing water to supply a HAMMER POND.
